# §R39.46 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: cost-safety read on `spec_digest`'s `stale → auto-resubmit`, plus the EpsInf/P5 re-run prices proposer8 asked for

Two requests answered together because they share one mechanism: what the harness inherits from a
previous round, and what it silently re-spends. Terms used below: `spec_digest` = coder12's new
sha256 over the plan entry's computation-defining fields, stored in the `submitted` marker and
compared before an idempotent skip; `pkg_fingerprint` = the pre-existing per-build hash that
`payload/common.sh::sei_stage` checks one level down, at stage-checkpoint granularity.

## PART 1 — cost-safety read on `stale → auto-resubmit` (for lead)

**Verdict: the `stale → auto-resubmit` choice is cost-safe as designed. I found three exposures,
none of them the one asked about, and the worst is in the opposite direction — a false NEGATIVE
that costs a wrong answer rather than core-h.**

### 1.1 The premise "the core-h is already reserved by preflight" — VERIFIED TRUE, structurally

`plan.py::build_plan()` takes no `store` argument and never consults marker state anywhere in its
body; `guard.reserve(item.key, core_hours=reserved, ...)` fires for every runnable item
unconditionally. `store.is_done(key)` is consulted only inside `cmd_submit`'s submission loop
(`cli.py:599`) — i.e. AFTER `cmd_preflight` has returned the reservation and after the guard has
already accepted or rejected against it. **A skipped item's ceiling is reserved exactly as if it
would run.** Confirmed against the returned artefact: `results/plan.json` lists all 11 items with
full budgets and `guard.core_hours_reserved: 11,297.39` includes the items that were skipped.

⟹ **An auto-resubmit can never push a round past a guard that round already passed.** coder12's
premise is not merely true today, it is true by construction, because the reservation path has no
access to the state it would need to be wrong.

### 1.2 Preflight snapshot vs submitted snapshot — no drift within a run

`cmd_submit` calls `cmd_preflight` itself and then iterates the identical `planned` list object.
`spec_digest(entry)` at `cli.py:603` and the digest written into the submitted marker at
`cli.py:833` read the same `entry` dict. **There is no path by which the reviewed entry and the
submitted entry differ inside one process.** The scenario lead raised is closed for the in-process
case.

Across invocations it is a different story, but it is pre-existing and not introduced here: a human
reads a `--dry-run` table on Monday and submits on Wednesday, and `build_plan` rebuilds from config
in between. What `spec_digest` changes is the CONSEQUENCE — a plan edit that previously produced a
silent skip now produces a resubmission. That is the intended behaviour; it just means the
reviewed-table-versus-submitted-table gap is now load-bearing where it used to be inert.

### 1.3 🔴 Exposure A — `cores_per_node` is in the digest and is environment-DETECTED

`SPEC_DIGEST_FIELDS` includes `cores_per_node`. `entry["cores_per_node"]` originates in
`cpn = cores_per_node or env.get("cores_per_node") or 32` — i.e. from `probe_node`'s detection, with
a hardcoded `32` fallback and a config-level `ncpus_override` on top. The returned report carries
`cores_per_node: 68`, `cores_per_node_source: "probe_node (run on a compute node)"`, and a separate
`cores_per_node_login_fallback` field — **the harness itself knows this number can come out
differently depending on where detection ran.**

⟹ **If a resume runs somewhere detection returns a different value, EVERY item's digest flips at
once, every done item reads `stale`, and the whole workdir auto-resubmits.** Guard-safe per §1.1,
so no ceiling breach — but on this workdir specifically that is roughly

```
P1b        595.5 core-h   \
P5      >=1003.4          | ~1,700 core-h of real re-spend
P6           6.2          | plus one full round of calendar
endpoints  108.4          /                                     silently, with no prompt
```

🟢 **Not urgent, and this is the part that makes the current design defensible**: every marker on
disk today lacks a `spec_digest` field, so all of them are `unknown` and skip-only. **Exposure A
cannot fire this round. It arms one round from now**, when the first digest-bearing markers exist.

Cheapest fixes, either is fine:
```
(a) drop `cores_per_node` from SPEC_DIGEST_FIELDS. The tuple's own docstring says fields that
    change WHERE/HOW a job runs "must not invalidate a done marker" — a detected core count is
    exactly that. One-line diff, removes the trigger entirely.
(b) if it must stay: cap the blast radius. Refuse to auto-resubmit when more than N items go stale
    in a single pass; print the table and require `--rerun`. A ONE-item flip is a plan edit; an
    ALL-items flip is an environment artefact. That distinction costs nothing to compute and is the
    whole difference between the fix working and the fix costing a round.
```

### 1.4 🔴🔴 Exposure B — the false NEGATIVE, and it is the worse direction: `SEI_QC_LEVEL` is not in the digest

`build_common_env` (`cli.py:697`) places `SEI_QC_LEVEL` — derived from `--level g1|g2`, the theory
level every payload runs at — into `common_env`. `common_env` is NOT `entry["extra_env"]` and is NOT
in `SPEC_DIGEST_FIELDS`.

⟹ **`./run.sh --level g2` against a workdir whose items are already done returns `match` on every
item, skips every item, and assembles a report from level-g1 results while the invocation said g2.**
The same hole covers `SEI_QC_MODULE` and `SEI_QC_LOGIN_PATH` (which Gaussian build executed).

This is the mirror image of the bug the fix was written for, on the single most
computation-defining knob in the package. Cost direction: it SAVES core-h and corrupts the answer —
and "a number correctly computed under a label that no longer describes it" is precisely the failure
class this project already caught once, in `criteria/p5.py`'s hardcoded level label. Fix is small:
fold `common_env` into the digest, or move `SEI_QC_LEVEL` into per-item `extra_env` where the digest
already sees it.

**This is the item I would not close the review on.** Exposure A costs a round; Exposure B costs a
result that looks fine.

### 1.5 🟡 Exposure C — wall-cap changes invalidate only by accident, via `chain_links`

Loosening a wall cap is the documented remedy for a BUDGET-class indeterminate ("a cap stopped it →
loosen the cap", the five-class taxonomy in `05_STATE.md` §3). The cap reaches the payload through
sizing, not through `extra_env`, so it does not enter the digest directly. `chain_links` IS in the
digest and IS derived from budget/wall — so a cap change flips the digest exactly when the rounding
happens to change the number of chained links, and not otherwise. Non-monotone, unpredictable
coverage.

The same inclusion also contradicts the tuple's stated intent: the docstring names "wall rounding"
as a WHERE/HOW field that must not invalidate, and `chain_links` is wall rounding's direct output.
So `chain_links` is simultaneously too weak for the case it accidentally covers and too strong for
the case the docstring names. One look, not a blocker.

### 1.6 🟡 What the design already contains, worth recording so it isn't rediscovered

`reset_item` deliberately leaves `jobs/<key>/stages/` intact, so an auto-resubmit resumes from stage
checkpoints when `pkg_fingerprint` matches — meaning a resubmit after a pure plan edit usually costs
only the changed stages, not the whole item. Good design, and it materially reduces Exposure A's
price whenever no rebuild intervened.

**But it does not protect the raw evidence.** The job directory is keyed by item name and reused, so
a resubmit overwrites the previous round's logs — the exact mechanism that destroyed P1's IRC logs
(§1a finding 6). An auto-resubmit therefore spends what it costs to re-run PLUS the unpriced loss of
the artefacts needed to diagnose why it went stale in the first place.
Mitigation is nearly free and matches a pattern already in the file: `reset_item` renames markers
rather than deleting them; do the same for `jobs/<key>` (rename to `<key>.reset.<epoch>`) before an
auto-resubmit. Cost: one `os.rename` and ~19 MB of scratch against 7,617 TB available.

## PART 2 — the re-run prices proposer8 asked for

### 2.1 Reconciling the two cost readings first

proposer8 priced from `jobs/*/stages/*.json` (stage wall × cores); §R39.45 priced from
`executions.jsonl` (job wall × cores) and from G16's own `Elapsed time` lines. All three agree and
the gaps are meaningful rather than noise:

```
                            stage marker   G16 internal   job level
endpoint rough (18.5 arm)      57.99          51.62
endpoint tight+freq             7.02           6.41
sum                            65.01          58.03          65.87
```
Stage minus G16-internal = per-stage setup; job minus stage-sum = 0.86 core-h of wrapper. **Use the
stage-marker numbers (proposer8's 65.0) as the charging basis** — they are what the harness bills.
The G16-internal split is only useful for the one thing it is used for below: separating the
frequency stage's 2.27 core-h from the tight optimisation's 4.14 inside the same stage marker.

### 2.2 Item 1 — "low arm alone ≈ 65 core-h": CORRECT, and it cannot be made cheaper

proposer8 is right that only the frequency stage reads `EpsInf`, and right that it is ~7 of the 65.
It does not follow that the low arm can be run for 7, and the reason is `pkg_fingerprint`, not
physics:

```
endpoint_prep_reactant/stages/*         pkg_fingerprint = 028acb21dc49701c
endpoint_prep_reactant_epsinf_full/*    pkg_fingerprint = 74a881b6f3bfa5cb
current source tree                     ~2fd3320c854a8f2d   [INDICATIVE — see caveat]
```

`sei_stage` inherits a completed stage only when `rc == 0` AND the marker's fingerprint equals the
current build's. The low arm's `endpoint_rough_reactant` marker carries a build that is neither of
the other two, so **it will not be inherited and the rough optimisation re-runs in full.**
⟹ **65 core-h, not 7. There is no cheap-resume option for the low arm.**

🟡 [INDICATIVE, not [MEASURED]] the `2fd3320c` value is computed over the source tree with a
`sei_pilot_work` subdirectory present, which the payload excludes at runtime, so the exact submit-time
value will differ. The CONCLUSION is safe regardless: `05_STATE.md` records a rebuild between these
rounds plus further source edits after it, and the two arms already disagree with each other.
Recommend coder12 simply print `sei_pkg_fingerprint` at submit time and stop anyone guessing.

### 2.3 Item 2 — "both arms, 130 core-h": APPROVED on cost grounds, with no argument required

```
both arms                             130 core-h
existing reservation for the pair     768 core-h  (2 x 384)  -> 5.9x headroom, ceiling does not move
this entire round's actual spend       73 core-h
guard                              21,000 core-h            -> 0.62%
```

130 core-h is below the level at which I have an opinion. proposer8 offered to take a disagreement
to lead; there is no disagreement to take. **Do not spend further effort justifying a 130 core-h
item against a 21,000 core-h guard** — the justification costs more than the compute.

Independently, and this strengthens his case rather than merely permitting it: §2.2 shows the low
arm re-runs under a THIRD build. So "low arm alone" does not merely risk a cross-build confound, it
**guarantees** one — the comparison would be 2fd3320c-rough against 74a881b6-rough. The confound
proposer8 was worried about is not hypothetical and not avoidable by spending less.

### 2.4 Item 3 — P5 frequency-only restart: the harness CANNOT do this today, and the reason is structural

`payload/P5.sh:90-92` builds one deck per species with route type `opt_freq` and wraps it in a
SINGLE checkpoint, `sei_stage "p5_${tag}"`. There is no optimisation/frequency stage boundary, so
there is nothing to restart from — and that stage's marker records the crash (`rc != 0`), so it
re-runs in full by design. Three changes are needed, all coder work, none a flag:

```
1. a `freq`-only route type in `sei_qc_input` (today: opt_freq)
2. read the starting geometry from the stored converged log instead of the packaged mol.xyz
3. split `sei_stage "p5_${tag}"` into `p5_${tag}_opt` / `p5_${tag}_freq`
```

Price of NOT building it, versus building it:
```
full P5 re-run (opt+freq, all species)      ~1,000-2,000 core-h   [ESTIMATE, from the 1,003.40
                                                                   measured opt-only floor]
frequency-only from stored geometries       ~46 / ~140 / ~600     [ESTIMATE, 13x spread, one
                                              (opt/base/pess)      measured Hessian as anchor]
saving                                      ~400-1,900 core-h
```
**Build it.** The saving exceeds the development cost by a wide margin, and change 3 (splitting the
stage) has value beyond this round: it makes every future P5 crash resumable at the granularity the
failure actually occurs at, which is the same lesson `stages_completed` already taught on the
reporting side.

### 2.5 proposer8's zero-cost pre-check — INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED, and it must gate any P5 round

Verified directly against `results/plan.json`, not taken on report:
```
endpoint_prep_reactant               extra_env has SEI_QC_EPSINF = 1.0
endpoint_prep_reactant_epsinf_full   extra_env has SEI_QC_EPSINF = 18.5
P5, P1b, P6_t1/t16/t64, all probes   extra_env = {}      <-- no EpsInf reaches them
```
Source confirms why: `plan.py:271` and `plan.py:690` set `SEI_QC_EPSINF` only for the two endpoint
bracket items, and `qc_adapter.sh:182` reads it from the environment, so an item without it in
`extra_env` emits a deck with no `EpsInf` line at all.

⟹ **A P5 recovery round submitted under the current plan crashes at the identical sentinel and
spends its entire budget producing nothing.** proposer8's framing is right and I am pricing nothing
for a P5 recovery until the plumbing lands. Concretely at risk if this is skipped: P5's 2,926 core-h
budget, ~1,000-2,000 of which would actually be spent before dying.

**Reported to**: team-lead (Part 1) and proposer8 (Part 2).

# §R39.47 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: design (C) repriced from measured stage internals — proposer8's 5–10 core-h CONFIRMED, with two implementation traps that would silently undo it

Repricing the endpoint EpsInf bracket after proposer8's §39.81 replaced design (A) (both arms
re-optimised, 130 core-h) with design (C) (both arms frequency-only from the stored
`endpoint_tight.chk`). Everything below comes from inside the one job that genuinely ran, so this is
a sharper estimate than §R39.45's, not a rescaled one.

## 1. New measurements extracted from `endpoint_tight.log`

```
NBasis, endpoint level3 (wB97XD/gen + PCM, 11 atoms)                   173      [MEASURED]
NBasis, P6 anchor level2 (same functional, same system, larger basis)  321      [MEASURED]
SCF cycle counts through the tight stage           19, 14, 10, 5, 1 cycles      [MEASURED]
smoke stage (two H2 jobs, L1 + L2)                     5.4 s + 5.9 s = 0.20 core-h
per-stage setup, tight stage (stage wall − G16 elapsed)              0.61 core-h
job wrapper (job wall − Σ stage walls, 48 s)                         0.85 core-h
```

🟢 **The `guess=read` restart is much cheaper than proposer8's conservative shape assumes, and the
cycle counts say so directly.** The tight stage's five SCFs run 19 → 14 → 10 → 5 → 1 cycles; the
final 1-cycle SCF is the in-job frequency stage inheriting a converged density, which is exactly the
step proposer8 correctly flags as absent from a restart. But a restart with `guess=read` does not
start cold either — it reads the **converged** density out of the checkpoint. The relevant bracket is
therefore "1–3 cycles (warm, the density is already the answer)" to "19 cycles (as cold as this
system ever gets, measured)", not "one cold SCF of unknown size".

Cost per SCF cycle, backed out of the same stage: step 1 spent 233.1 s covering 48 SCF cycles, one
`CalcFC` Hessian and ~4 gradients; step 2 spent 127.6 s covering 1 SCF cycle plus the full analytic
Hessian and CPHF. Subtracting a Hessian's worth leaves ≈1.5–2 s per SCF cycle at 64 threads.

## 2. Design (C) priced

```
per arm                                            core-h        basis
-----------------------------------------------   ---------     ---------------------------------
frequency / Hessian / CPHF                            2.27       [MEASURED] step 2's own elapsed
SCF re-convergence from guess=read                0.04–0.71      [ESTIMATE] 1–19 cycles × 1.5–2 s
per-stage setup                                       0.61       [MEASURED] tight stage
smoke (H2, L1+L2)                                     0.20       [MEASURED]
job wrapper                                           0.85       [MEASURED]
-----------------------------------------------   ---------
per arm                                           3.97–4.64
TWO ARMS                                          7.9 –9.3 core-h
```

**proposer8's `≈5–10 core-h` is CONFIRMED — measured-basis range 7.9–9.3, sitting in the upper half
of the band he offered.** No revision requested and none needed. Note where the money actually is:
of ~4.3 core-h per arm, only ~2.6 is physics; ~1.7 is smoke, setup and wrapper. **At this size the
harness costs almost as much as the calculation** — which is fine at 9 core-h and is the reason
neither arm should be sized whole-node (see trap 2).

Against the pair's existing reservation of 768 core-h this is **1.2%**; against the 21,000 guard,
**0.04%**. The bracket has ceased to be a budget question entirely.

🟢 **The P6 anchor is NOT a usable proxy for the restart SCF, and the reason is worth recording so
nobody substitutes it**: it runs at NBasis 321 against the endpoint's 173, so its 3.13 core-h is a
different-sized calculation, not a same-sized one. Scaled down it would give ~0.5–0.9 core-h, which
is consistent with the cycle-count route above but strictly weaker evidence. Use the cycle counts.

## 3. Contingency line, carried as proposer8 asked

```
design (A) fallback — fires iff the two arms' printed force matrices differ    130 core-h + 1 round
```
Carried, not deleted. My own read of the odds is that it will not fire (proposer8's line-number
evidence that `NEqPCM` is matched zero times in the rough log and only at the `calcfc` and `freq`
sites in the tight log is stronger than a plausibility argument), but a 130 core-h contingency
against a 21,000 guard costs nothing to carry and everything to have deleted if it fires.

## 4. 🔴 Trap 1 — implementing (C) as a flag on `endpoint_prep.sh` silently restores design (A)'s price

`endpoint_prep.sh` runs `endpoint_rough_reactant` then `endpoint_tight_reactant`. If design (C) ships
as a flag on that payload, the rough stage is still IN the script, and `sei_stage` will skip it only
when the stored marker's `pkg_fingerprint` matches the current build. It does not — the two existing
arms already carry different fingerprints (`028acb21dc49701c` / `74a881b6f3bfa5cb`) and the source
has moved again since. **The rough optimisation would re-run, turning a 4 core-h arm into a ~62
core-h arm, per arm, with no error and no warning** — the checkpoint would log
`rerun_stale_fingerprint` and proceed.

⟹ **design (C) must be a payload with no rough stage in it at all, not a flag on the existing one.**
This is not a style preference: the cheap version and the expensive version differ by 15× and the
harness will silently choose the expensive one.

## 5. 🔴 Trap 2 — whole-node sizing would reserve ~30× the work, and both arms must share a thread count

Two separate points that happen to share a fix.

**(a) Sizing.** ADR-110's rule applies in spirit: an Item doing ~4 core-h of work, sized whole-node
(64 cores) against a `min_wall_h` floor of 0.5 h, reserves 32 core-h per arm. Not a spend, but it is
the third time this shape has appeared (the xtb anchor, B+'s terminal optimisations, now here).
**Declare `cores_per_task` explicitly.**

**(b) 🔴 The thread count is not free to vary, because proposer8's tightened criterion is tight.**
§39.81 sets `|ΔE| ≤ 1e-7 Hartree` and `|Δν| ≤ 0.1 cm⁻¹`. Gaussian's parallel reductions are
deterministic for a fixed thread count but not necessarily across thread counts, so **running the two
arms at different thread counts could manufacture a difference at exactly the magnitude the
criterion is testing.** Both arms must run at the same thread count, on the same declared core count.
Free to enforce, expensive to discover afterwards.

🟢 **And the criterion is attainable — measured, not assumed.** Three separate SCFs at the converged
geometry inside the tight stage (log lines 2259, 2640, 3516; 10, 5 and 1 cycles respectively) all
return `-349.620897959` Hartree — agreement to **1e-9 Hartree**, i.e. the same value proposer8
quotes. So the same-node, same-thread-count reproducibility floor is ~100× tighter than the 1e-7
criterion. What is NOT measured is cross-job/cross-node reproducibility.

🟢 **Which makes proposer8's constraint 3 sharper than "plumbing control", and it should be read
first.** Arm F reproducing `-349.620897959` across a different job, a different node and a different
build IS the cross-job reproducibility measurement, and it now has an in-job floor of 1e-9 to be
compared against. **If arm F cannot reproduce it to 1e-7, the correct response is to report the
achievable floor, not to loosen the criterion after seeing the data** — and no verdict may be read
from the U-versus-F comparison, exactly as §39.81 already requires. Costs nothing; it is a reading
order, not a calculation.

## 6. Round-total effect

I do not hold the next round's full item list, so these are deltas against whatever it turns out to be.

```
NEW SPEND
  endpoint EpsInf bracket, design (C), both arms          7.9–9.3 core-h   [MEASURED basis]
  16-thread packing validation (lead-approved)               ~24 core-h    [ESTIMATE]
  one P5 species at both EpsInf values (§39.81 addition)    ~2–100 core-h  [ESTIMATE — see note]
  P5 frequency recovery, design (B), IF plumbing lands      46/140/600     [ESTIMATE, 13× spread]
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  floor (bracket + validation only)                            ~33 core-h
  everything runs, base case                                  ~200 core-h
  everything runs, pessimistic                                ~730 core-h

RESERVATION CHANGES (no spend, ceiling only)
  P6 resize 24 h → 2 h cap                                 −1,782 core-h
  U56-2 endpoint certs at ~130 core-h each                   −760 core-h
  endpoint bracket pair                                    no change needed (768 already reserved,
                                                            1.2% of it will be used)

CONTINGENCY, carried not spent
  design (A) fallback if the force matrices differ         +130 core-h + 1 round
```

🔴 **Note on the "one P5 species at both EpsInf values" line, because the species choice moves the
price by 50×.** A small closed-shell species costs ~1 core-h per arm; `li_ec2_cation` — the species
whose optimisation alone measured 429.55 core-h and did not converge in 49 cycles — has an unmeasured
frequency cost that could plausibly run 10–50 core-h per arm. **This is proposer8's choice to make,
not mine, and the cost is not the deciding factor at either end** (both are affordable). Flagging
only so the species is chosen deliberately rather than by whichever one the loop reaches first.

🔴 **Still not priceable: the P5 recovery itself.** `results/plan.json` shows `extra_env = {}` for
P5, so a recovery round under the current plan crashes at the identical sentinel and spends its whole
budget producing nothing (§R39.46 §2.5). The 46/140/600 line above is conditional on the plumbing
landing first; it is not a commitment.

**Reported to**: team-lead and proposer8.

# §R39.48 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: the `ec_radical_anion` EpsInf pair priced — and a SELF-CORRECTION to my own P5 frequency-only estimate, which was under-anchored by ~4×

Answering lead's question about §39.82's spot-check species. Getting the answer required pulling
`NBasis` out of every P5 species log, and doing that exposed an error in my own §R39.46/§R39.47 P5
number. **The correction is reported first, because the species answer depends on it.**

## 1. 🔴🔴 SELF-CORRECTION — my P5 frequency-only estimate was anchored on the wrong basis set

§R39.46 §2.4 and §R39.47 both quote P5 frequency-only recovery at **~46 / ~140 / ~600 core-h**. That
range is WRONG and wrong in the expensive direction. The mistake:

```
the measured Hessian anchor (2.27 core-h)   endpoint tight stage, level3, NBasis = 173
what P5 actually runs                       level2, NBasis = 74 to 620 — mostly 299-620
```

I priced P5's species as "the 11-atom class" and scaled by atom count. **P5 does not run at the
endpoint's level.** `ec_radical_anion` has ten atoms — one FEWER than the anchor — and NBasis 299
against the anchor's 173, because level2 carries a substantially larger basis. Scaling by atom count
made the anchor look applicable when the cost driver had moved by 1.7× underneath it.

🔒 **This is the S₂₁ cube-law error (§R39.41) repeated by me, in the same document that retracted
it.** Same shape exactly: scaling a measured cost by atom count when atom count is not the driver.
proposer7 caught it in engineer7's numbers; nobody caught it in mine — I found it only because lead
asked a question that forced me to read `NBasis` per species. Recording it as a finding rather than
editing the old numbers quietly.

### Corrected P5 frequency-only estimate

Model: `Hessian ≈ 2.27 core-h × (NBasis/173)^p × (3N/33)`, anchored on the one measured Hessian,
with `p` bracketed by real data rather than assumed:

```
p = 2.2   empirically calibrated: the P6 anchor (NBasis 321) took 25 SCF cycles in 171.7 s
          = 6.9 s/cycle at 64 threads, against ~1.75 s/cycle at NBasis 173 (backed out of the
          endpoint tight stage). ln(3.93)/ln(1.855) = 2.22.       [MEASURED, 2 points]
p = 3.0   conventional upper bound for the CPHF/derivative-integral part, which is steeper than
          the SCF part the two measured points describe.          [LITERATURE-shaped, not measured]
p = 2.6   midpoint, used as the base case.
```

```
                              p=2.2      p=2.6      p=3.0
P5 frequency-only, 22 rows    375        577        901   core-h
previously quoted by me        46        140        600   core-h   ← WRONG, under-anchored
```

Per-species, base case (p = 2.6), which is also the table anyone sizing a future P5 round should use:
```
li_ec2_cation_s0/s1_L2   NBasis 620   ~119.7 each      ec_s0_L1              NBasis 267   ~6.4
ec_dimer_s0_L2           NBasis 598   ~103.8           pf6_anion_s0_L2       NBasis 288   ~5.4
li_ec2_cation_s0_L1      NBasis 551    ~88.1           hco3_anion_s0_L2      NBasis 174   ~1.1
emc_radical_anion/emc_s0 NBasis 404    ~28.1 each      c2h4_s0_L2            NBasis 142   ~0.7
emc_s0_L1                NBasis 340    ~17.9           ch3o_radical_s0/s1    NBasis 128   ~0.5 each
li_ec_cation / li_ec_rad NBasis 321    ~11.3 each      co2_s0_L1/L2          NBasis 117   ~0.2 each
ec_radical_anion ×2, ec_s0/s1_L2 NBasis 299 ~8.6 each  h2o_s0_L2             NBasis  74   ~0.07
```
**Four species carry 70% of the cost.** That is a lever if the recovery ever needs cutting — and it
is a much better-shaped problem than a flat 22-way spend.

### What the correction does and does not change

```
🟢 design (B) is STILL worth building. Full P5 re-run ~1,000–2,000 core-h vs frequency-only
   ~375–900. Saving ~100–1,600 core-h, plus every future P5 crash becomes resumable at the
   granularity the failure occurs at. The recommendation stands.
🔴 the MARGIN is thinner than I said. I claimed ~400–1,900 saved; the honest figure is ~100–1,600,
   and at the pessimistic end of (B) against the optimistic end of (A) the saving is small.
🔴 nobody should have been planning against the 46/140/600 numbers. They appear in §R39.46 §2.4,
   §R39.47 §6, and in messages to lead and proposer8 on 2026-08-21. Superseded by this section.
```

## 2. `ec_radical_anion` — the answer lead asked for

Per-arm build-up, freq-only from the stored checkpoint (`species/ec_radical_anion_s0_L2/job.chk`,
10.5 MB, present; `Optimization completed` / `Stationary point found` both confirmed in its log, so a
`geom=check guess=read` restart is viable — this was checked, not assumed):

```
                                      optimistic     base      pessimistic     basis
Hessian / CPHF (NBasis 299, 3N=30)        6.88        8.56        10.65        p=2.2/2.6/3.0
SCF re-convergence from guess=read        0.10        0.60         1.90        1–19 cycles
                                                                               @ ~5.8 s/cycle
per-stage setup + smoke + wrapper         1.66        1.66         1.66        [MEASURED]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
per arm                                   8.64       10.82        14.21
PAIR (two arms)                          17.3        21.6         28.4  core-h
```

**Against the ~20 core-h threshold: the pair STRADDLES it. Optimistic 17.3 clears; base 21.6 does
not; pessimistic 28.4 is 1.4× over. By the rule as written, the fallback triggers.**

`hco3_anion` for comparison — and it is genuinely cheap, not marginally cheaper:
```
Hessian / CPHF (NBasis 174 ≈ the anchor's 173, 3N=15)      ~1.05 core-h, flat across all three p
SCF re-convergence                                          0.03–0.60
setup + smoke + wrapper                                          1.66
per arm                                                     2.74–3.31
PAIR                                                        5.5 –6.6 core-h
```
Its NBasis of 174 sits one function away from the measured anchor's 173, so its estimate carries far
less model risk than `ec_radical_anion`'s — that is worth knowing independently of which is chosen.

## 3. 🔴 My recommendation: raise the threshold, do not switch the species

The number says switch. **I think the rule is wrong, not the species, and I would rather say so than
hand back a number that quietly makes a scientific decision.**

```
the difference between the two species             ~16 core-h
this round's total new spend, base case           ~200 core-h
the P5 recovery this spot-check exists to qualify  375–900 core-h
the guard                                       21,000 core-h    ⟹ the pair is 0.10% of it
```

A 16 core-h delta cannot carry a species choice. And the two species are not near-substitutes:
`ec_radical_anion` is an anion AND an open-shell doublet AND has soft modes AND is the actual S1
reduction intermediate — the maximum reaction-field coupling case, which is the entire reason a
spot-check exists. `hco3_anion` is a rigid five-atom **closed-shell** anion; it retains the charge
axis and drops the open-shell and soft-mode axes, which is most of what is being tested.

**Concretely: raise the threshold to ~200 core-h.** That is where a spot-check starts competing with
the recovery it is meant to qualify, and it is the first point at which I would object on cost
grounds. Below it, science decides. If proposer8 prefers to keep a bright line at 20, that is a
legitimate call and `hco3_anion` at ~6 core-h is fine — but it should be made knowing the budget is
not what is forcing it.

## 4. Two constraints that carry over from §R39.47, unchanged

```
- both arms at the SAME thread count. §39.81's |ΔE| ≤ 1e-7 Hartree is tight enough that a
  thread-count difference could manufacture a difference at the tested magnitude.
- do NOT implement as a flag on P5.sh. Its single `sei_stage "p5_${tag}"` marker records rc != 0
  and will re-run the whole opt+freq — turning a ~11 core-h arm back into a ~20+ core-h one, and
  worse for the larger species. This is the same trap as §R39.47 §4, one payload over.
```
🟢 And the P5 spot-check needs no new machinery beyond changes 1–3 already recommended for the
recovery (freq-only route type, geometry from the stored log/checkpoint, opt/freq stage split) —
proposer8 is right that one build serves the endpoint bracket, the P5 recovery AND this spot-check.
**Price it as one effort, not three.**

**Reported to**: team-lead and proposer8.

# §R39.49 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: proposer8's one-job design has a silent `%chk` collision that breaks their own constraint 1; and P5's recovery splits 17/5, not 20/20

Two findings from checking §39.85's one-job design and from the convergence audit proposer8's own
species check prompted. Both were found by reading the returned artefacts, not by reasoning about the
design.

## 1. 🔴🔴 The one-job / two-`Link1`-step design silently violates constraint 1 unless `%oldchk` is used

proposer8's §39.85(1) is right on the physics — a different CPU can manufacture a 1e-7 difference the
same way a different thread count can, so putting both arms in one job on one node makes every
variable common-mode. **I agree with the design and with superseding engineer8's separate-tasks rule
for this item.** The wall arithmetic checks out: ~0.14 h serial against a 6 h cap is 2%, and the
failure mode (job dies, both arms die, ~9 core-h to redo) is correctly priced as acceptable.

**But the mechanism collides with constraint 1.** Constraint 1 says both arms must be fresh from the
SAME stored density — never one seeded from the other's output, because unrestricted SCF solutions
are not unique and a shared bias must stay common-mode. In a single G16 job:

```
the only %chk line in the endpoint deck today:   %chk=endpoint_tight.chk       (one, shared)
step 1 (arm U) runs with geom=check guess=read   -> reads the stored density   ✅
step 1 finishes                                  -> WRITES its converged density back to that chk
step 2 (arm F) runs with geom=check guess=read   -> reads ARM U's output       🔴 constraint 1 broken
```

**Arm F would be seeded from arm U's converged density instead of the original checkpoint** — the
exact asymmetry constraint 1 exists to forbid, introduced by the mechanism chosen to enforce
constraint 4, and it would leave no trace in the output. A reader would see two arms, one job, one
node, one build and conclude the comparison was maximally controlled.

**Fix, and it is small**: give each step its own output checkpoint and read the original through
Gaussian's `%OldChk`:
```
step 1:   %oldchk=endpoint_tight.chk   %chk=arm_u.chk    geom=check guess=read   EpsInf=1.0
step 2:   %oldchk=endpoint_tight.chk   %chk=arm_f.chk    geom=check guess=read   EpsInf=18.5
```
Both steps then read the same untouched stored density and write elsewhere. 🟡 `%OldChk` is
documented G16 Link0 behaviour but this package has never emitted it — **coder12 must verify it
against a real deck rather than trusting this note**, and the cheapest verification is the run
itself: if arm F reproduces `-349.620897959` (constraint 3) the plumbing is right, and if it does not
this is the first thing to check.

🟡 **Second, smaller implementation note on the same design: the package has never emitted an explicit
`--Link1--` block.** The endpoint deck contains zero `Link1` strings; its two internal job steps came
from G16 splitting an `opt ... freq` route on its own. So the two-`Link1`-steps-in-one-job shape is a
deck feature that does not exist yet, and proposer8's stated fallback (same-node placement with the
host recorded in both arms' records) may end up being the primary path rather than the fallback.
**Cost impact either way: none** — both shapes cost the same core-h. Flagging only so the fallback is
built deliberately rather than discovered.

🟢 One cost improvement the one-job design does buy, unasked: setup, smoke and wrapper are paid ONCE
rather than twice. The endpoint pair drops from **7.9–9.3 to ~7.3–8.6 core-h**. Immaterial, recorded
for accuracy.

## 2. 🔴🔴 P5's recovery splits 17 / 5, and the 5 are the five most expensive rows

proposer8 checked `li_ec2_cation`'s log before choosing a spot-check species and found it never
reached the frequency stage — its optimisation never converged, so design (C)/(B) cannot touch it at
any price. **That check generalises, and I ran it across all 22 rows.** Result:

```
17 rows   "Stationary point found" = 1, "EpsInf not defined" = 1
          ⟹ converged, THEN died at the frequency stage. Recoverable frequency-only. ✅
 5 rows   "Stationary point found" = 0, "EpsInf not defined" = 0
          ⟹ never reached the frequency stage at all. NOT an EpsInf casualty. ❌
            li_ec2_cation_s0_L2   NBasis 620   (stage marker present, 429.55 core-h, 49 cycles)
            li_ec2_cation_s1_L2   NBasis 620   (no stage marker — one of the two wall-killed tasks)
            ec_dimer_s0_L2        NBasis 598   (stage marker present)
            li_ec2_cation_s0_L1   NBasis 551   (no stage marker — the other wall-killed task)
            emc_radical_anion_s0_L2 NBasis 404 (stage marker present)
```

**The five non-recoverable rows are the five largest basis sets in the set.** Corrected recovery
estimate, replacing §R39.48's own figures for the second time today:

```
                                                    p=2.2    p=2.6    p=3.0
17 converged rows, frequency-only  (design (B))       92      118      152   core-h
 5 non-converged rows, Hessian cost IF they ever
   converge — NOT a recovery cost, a future cost     282      459      749   core-h
 all 22, as §R39.48 quoted                           375      577      901   core-h
```

### What this changes, stated plainly

```
🟢 design (B) gets CHEAPER and much better-bounded: ~92–152 core-h, not 375–901. The 13x spread
   collapses to 1.7x, because the rows carrying the model risk (the 1.7-3.6x NBasis extrapolations
   from the measured anchor) are exactly the rows that turn out to be unrecoverable. Build it.
🔴 "one EpsInf fix recovers P5" is true for 17 of 20 attempted rows, not all of them. The other
   three (plus the two wall-killed) were never blocked by EpsInf — they are blocked by optimisation
   non-convergence, which is U-55's floppy-PES problem with a DIFFERENT prescription (conformer
   quality, per proposer7's §39.72(3): li_ec2_cation's scf_max=14 was fine, its opt=49 was not).
   05_STATE.md §1a's "P5 is half-collected, not void" holds; "one fix recovers FOUR items
   simultaneously" needs the 17/20 qualifier attached wherever it is quoted.
🔴 my §R39.48 per-species table listed li_ec2_cation ×2 and ec_dimer as "four species carry 70% of
   the cost". That is arithmetically right and operationally misleading: those species are not in
   the recovery at all. The 70% figure should not be used as a cutting lever — there is nothing to
   cut, they were never in scope.
🔴 the 5 rows' real cost is an OPTIMISATION problem, and it is not small: li_ec2_cation_s0_L2 alone
   already burned 429.55 core-h without converging in 49 cycles. Re-running them as-is buys another
   429 core-h of the same. Anything spent here should follow the conformer-quality prescription, not
   a longer wall cap — and it should be priced separately, when someone asks, not folded into the
   EpsInf recovery where it does not belong.
```

🔒 **This is the third time today the same shape has caught one of my numbers**: a statistic computed
over the rows that were AVAILABLE rather than over the rows the question was about. §39.51(a)'s
success-conditioned-denominator concern, arriving on the cost side. I did not catch it; proposer8's
species check did, and only because they verified a disqualification against the logs instead of
accepting my price for it.

## 3. Nothing above changes the species choice or the spot-check price

`ec_radical_anion_s0_L2` is in the converged 17, has its checkpoint on disk, and its pair price is
unchanged at **17.3 / 21.6 / 28.4 core-h** (§R39.48 §2) — less the shared-overhead saving from §1
above if the one-job design is used, which brings it to roughly **16.6 / 20.9 / 27.7**. Under the
one-job design the base case lands at 20.9 against a ~20 threshold: still straddling, still not a
budget question, recommendation from §R39.48 §3 unchanged (raise the threshold to ~200, do not
switch species). proposer8 has since disqualified the expensive alternative on evidence rather than
cost, which settles it independently.

**Reported to**: team-lead and proposer8.

# §R39.50 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: coder12's three auto-resubmit questions, priced from measured spend

Answering the three questions coder12 put directly. All blast radii below are `[MEASURED]` from this
round's returned tree, not reasoned from budgets — the difference matters, because in every case the
budget figure and the real figure differ by 2–3×.

## Q1 — worst case for rule (i): is a retry counter worth the mechanism?

### The real worst case is ~1,000–2,000 core-h per round, not "up to 3,128"

```
P5 reserved                                                     3,127.59 core-h
P5 spend before crashing on the EpsInf defect, MEASURED           988.52 core-h
  (Σ of the 20 stage markers — every one completed its optimisation, then died at freq)
plus the two wall-killed tasks, upper bound 2 × 496.6            +993.2  core-h
⟹ a P5 auto-resubmit against a persistent plumbing defect        ~1,000–1,980 core-h PER ROUND
```
The item does not fail fast. It fails *late*, after paying for everything except the stage that
breaks — which is the worst shape for an automatic retry, and it is the shape this specific defect
has.

### But the deciding argument is not the size, it is the expected yield of the classes in (i)

Rule (i) fires on `cause_class ∈ {protocol, engine, unknown}`. Taking the project's own definitions:

```
protocol  "our procedure was wrong -> fix the procedure". Resubmitting the SAME procedure
          reproduces the SAME outcome deterministically.        expected yield of a blind retry: ~0
engine    numerical failure internal to the electronic-structure method. The one measured instance
          (GFN2 rc=128) was proven path-sensitive and environment-dependent and did NOT reproduce
          standalone, 3/3.                                       genuinely nonzero — n = 1
unknown   missing completion record.                             undefined by construction
```
**Two of the three classes have no reason to succeed on an unchanged retry, and the third has one
data point.** A retry rule that fires regardless of whether anything changed is buying ~1,000 core-h
per round against a mechanism with ~0 expected yield in its dominant class.

### 🟢 Recommendation: not a counter — gate (i) on `pkg_fingerprint` having CHANGED

```
auto-resubmit on (i)  iff  the done marker's pkg_fingerprint differs from the current build's
```
Why this and not a retry counter:
```
- it expresses the actual precondition ("something changed that could plausibly fix it") directly,
  instead of approximating it with a count
- pkg_fingerprint is ALREADY computed (common.sh::sei_pkg_fingerprint) and ALREADY written into
  stage markers. No new state, no counter field, no increment, no reset rule.
- a counter needs a reset rule, and the only correct reset rule is "reset when something changed"
  — i.e. the counter design ends up reinventing this test, with extra state
- it bounds the worst case at exactly ONE re-spend per build, which is the correct semantics
- it closes rule (i)'s own justification gap precisely: spec_digest deliberately EXCLUDES
  pkg_fingerprint, so a source-only fix (P5.sh edited, plan unchanged) flips nothing today and
  (i) is the only thing that would rerun it. Under this gate that case fires — correctly — and a
  persistent defect with no source change never does.
```
🟡 Stated cost of the choice: `pkg_fingerprint` flips on ANY rebuild, including unrelated ones, so
after every rebuild each `protocol`/`engine`/`unknown` item retries once. Today that set is small and
bounded. **If it ever grows, add the counter then** — not now.
🟡 It also blocks the one case with real yield: an `engine` failure that is environment-dependent and
might succeed on a blind retry. Judgement: `--rerun KEY` is one command, preflight already prints the
item, and the measured `engine` instance cost ~0 (a GFN2 scan). **Do not build a cheap-item exception
until somebody is actually blocked by its absence** — an exception carved by budget size would need a
tuned constant, which this project has spent the round removing from elsewhere.

## Q2 — array granularity: NOT acceptable as-is, and I own part of the problem

### Measured blast radius

```
P5, one task with an `engine` outcome resubmits all 20        988.52 core-h to recover one task
worst single task in that set (li_ec2_cation_s0_L2)           429.55 core-h
cheapest task in that set (h2o_s0_L2)                           1.53 core-h
⟹ recovering h2o at item granularity costs 988.52 — an amplification of 646x
```

🔴 **And the "19 good ones re-run from scratch" part is caused by my own recommendation.** §R39.46
§1.6 asked for `jobs/<key>/` to be archived alongside the markers, to stop a resubmit overwriting the
previous round's raw evidence (the mechanism that destroyed P1's IRC logs). That is right on its own
terms and **it is exactly what destroys the stage checkpoints that would have made a resubmit
cheap.** Evidence preservation and cheap resume are in direct tension here and I did not see it when
I made the recommendation. Recording that rather than quietly reconciling it.

### 🟢 Recommendation, cheapest sufficient version

```
gate auto-resubmit on n_tasks in (None, 1). Array items NEVER auto-resubmit — print the failing
task IDs and require `--rerun KEY`.
```
One condition, no task-level submission machinery, and it puts the human decision exactly where the
amplification is 646×. Non-array items keep auto-resubmit, where a resubmit costs at most that item's
own budget by construction.

**Do not build task-level resubmission now.** `state.py` already has `task_marker_states()` and
`expected_task_count()`, so the state half exists — the missing half is submitting an arbitrary index
SET rather than a range, which PBS `-J` may not express. That is real work for a case a `--rerun`
covers today.

🟡 Optional, resolves the tension I created, ~20 small JSON files of I/O: after renaming
`jobs/<key>` → `jobs/<key>.reset.<epoch>`, copy the `stages/` subtree back into the fresh directory.
The existing `pkg_fingerprint` check then decides inheritance correctly, using tested machinery.
Narrow win — it only helps when the resubmit is plan-only with no rebuild, since after a rebuild the
fingerprints mismatch and everything re-runs anyway. Worth doing, not worth blocking on.

## Q3 — does the `cores_per_node` probe return a different value on resubmission? YES, four ways

Traced to `cli.py::build_env` (lines 75–130). **`cores_per_node` is re-probed live on every
invocation** — from the login node via `sinfo`/`pbsnodes` — and is never cached in a marker or file.
Its value comes from a four-way fallback chain, and **every branch can change between rounds on the
same cluster without the computation changing at all**:

```
1. --cores-per-node CLI override            a human passing the flag on one invocation and not the
                                            next. Most likely in practice — someone debugging.
2. max() over sinfo partitions / pbsnodes   a partition appearing, a node class drained or added.
                                            Site-side, no local change at all.
3. config/sizing.json usable_cores map      68 -> 64 on this cluster. A config edit flips it
                                            (this one is a legitimate change).
4. LOGIN-NODE core count, if the compute-node query fails for any reason
```
🔴 **Branch 4 is not hypothetical and the code says so in its own comment: "login 24 core / compute 68
(64 used) — a 2.7x difference."** One momentarily unavailable or permission-denied `pbsnodes` call
silently substitutes 24 for 64, **every item's digest flips at once, and the whole workdir
auto-resubmits.**

🟢 **And the code already computes the fact that would prevent this**: `cores_per_node_is_login_fallback`
is emitted into the report and never consulted. Another "measured but unread", this time in the field
that gates a re-spend.

### 🟢 The real defect, and the two-line fix

`cores_per_node` is doing double duty in the entry dict:
```
item declares cores_per_task (P6: 1/16/64)  -> entry["cores_per_node"] = that declaration
                                               COMPUTATION-DEFINING (it is P6's measurement)
item declares nothing (P5, P1b)             -> entry["cores_per_node"] = the probed value
                                               NOT computation-defining — WHERE/HOW only
```
One field, two meanings, and the digest cannot tell them apart. So including it protects P6 and
holds P5/P1b hostage to a probe, in the same line.

```
FIX:  remove "cores_per_node" from SPEC_DIGEST_FIELDS
      add    "cores_per_task"   (the Item's own declaration: None or an int)
```
P6 keeps full protection — its declaration is what matters and it is now in the digest under its own
name. P5/P1b stop being hostage to a login-node fallback. This also satisfies the tuple's own
docstring, which says WHERE/HOW fields must not invalidate a done marker. **Two lines, and it removes
the mass-resubmit trigger entirely** — better than the blast-radius cap I proposed in §R39.46 §1.3,
which was treating the symptom.

🔴 Unchanged and still open from §R39.46 §1.4: **`SEI_QC_LEVEL` is still not in the digest**, so
`--level g2` against a done workdir skips everything and reports g1 results. That is the
false-negative direction and it is the one that costs a wrong answer rather than core-h.

**Reported to**: coder12 (direct), team-lead.

# §R39.51 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: Round A priced, and its cross-build confound is already discharged — one arm, not two

proposer8's §39.88(3) reports a lead-approved Round A (design (A), today) / Round B (design (C),
built properly) split, with (A) rescoped to answer only the PRIMARY question (`n_imag`, an integer
count) and its ΔE/Δν pre-registered as "not resolved at this design's floor (≈5 meV)". Pricing that,
plus one result that halves it.

## 1. 🟢 Round A needs NO coder work and can go today

The blocker was never the plan. `results/plan.json` already carries
`endpoint_prep_reactant.extra_env.SEI_QC_EPSINF = '1.0'` — the arm was skipped by a stale done
marker, not by missing plumbing. **`./run.sh --rerun endpoint_prep_reactant` moves the markers aside
and resubmits, today, with zero dependency on the `spec_digest` work or on coder12's queue.**
`reset_item` is the documented path for exactly this and it renames rather than deletes.

⟹ Round A is decoupled from every other item in flight. It does not wait on anything.

## 2. 🟢🟢 The cross-build confound is EMPIRICALLY EXCLUDED, at zero cost, using proposer8's own comparator

The worry that would force two arms: the two existing job directories were produced by different
builds (`028acb21dc49701c` / `74a881b6f3bfa5cb`) and the newer one runs a start-selection path the
older lacks, so a re-run of the low arm alone could land in a different basin — making an `n_imag`
difference report the basin rather than `EpsInf`. That is a real confound for an integer comparison,
not only for the ΔE/Δν pair.

**Tested on the artefacts already on disk, using §39.70's ruled comparator (identical covalent
graphs, cation contacts excluded):**

```
elements identical                                        yes
covalent graph, base arm vs full arm       IDENTICAL, 10 bonds each
Li nearest contact (reported covariate, NOT a decision input)
     base 1.865 A (O5) / 2.830 (C0) / 3.097 (O1)
     full 1.861 A (O5) / 2.844 (C0) / 3.110 (O1)          agree to 0.004-0.014 A
max single-atom displacement                              0.2526 A  (a hydrogen)
```

🟢 **The two builds land in the SAME basin.** The 0.25 Å is a hydrogen rotation inside one minimum,
not a different structure — exactly what a covalent-graph comparator exists to distinguish, and the
distinction proposer8's §39.70 ruling was written to make.

🟡 **Honest limit, stated because it is the only thing that keeps this from being proof**: these are
the ROUGH-stage exit geometries, which is where the two builds actually differ (start selection). The
tight stage starts from the rough exit, so same-basin at the rough exit implies same-basin at
convergence under any ordinary optimiser behaviour — but that is an inference, not a measurement. It
is a strong inference and it costs nothing to make; it is not a certificate.

given rather than a point. Tight stage ~7.0, wrapper ~0.9. `[MEASURED]` on both endpoints of the

```

# §R39.52 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: U56-2 cert sizing corrected (my "3 × 384" was wrong), the level2 control priced, and a mass-flip trigger I created while removing one

## 1. 🔴 CORRECTION — my "U56-2's 3 endpoint certs, 1,152 core-h, −760" was wrong

coder12 asked which three items I meant. Reading `plan.py`'s U56-2 set, the answer exposes an error
in my own number:

```
endpoint_prep_reactant        11-atom   explicit_wall_h 6.0, whole-node ->    384 core-h
endpoint_prep_product         11-atom   explicit_wall_h 6.0, whole-node ->    384
endpoint_prep_rc_reactant     21-atom   lead ruling §R26.1              ->  1,536  (24 h)
                                                                          -------
                                                                            2,304 core-h
```
**I quoted 3 × 384 = 1,152.** The set is not homogeneous — one member is a 21-atom item reserved at
four times the others. 🔒 **Third occurrence today of the same shape**: a statistic over a set I
assumed uniform without checking (after the atom-count-vs-basis anchor error and the
available-rows-vs-relevant-rows denominator). The mechanical rule proposer8 gave me — name the
variable you are scaling by and verify it differs between anchor and target — would have caught this
one too, if I had applied it to a *set* rather than only to a scaled estimate. Extending it: **name
the variable, and verify the set is uniform in it.**

### Corrected recommendation

```
11-atom certs (endpoint_prep_reactant, endpoint_prep_product)
   measured cost 65.87 core-h, measured wall 1.029 h                    [MEASURED, n=1]
   RECOMMEND wall 6 h -> 3 h  = 192 core-h reserved each
   recovers 2 × (384 - 192) = 384 core-h

21-atom cert (endpoint_prep_rc_reactant)
   🔴 DO NOT TOUCH. Leave 1,536 core-h / 24 h exactly as lead ruled.
```

**Why 3 h and not the 2 h my "~130 core-h" implied.** 2 h × 64 = 128 core-h, which is where that
figure came from, and it is 1.94× the measured wall. But three facts argue for more headroom:
```
- n = 1. The only other endpoint attempt this project has made crashed.
- the same molecule at the same level took 33m59s in one arm and 48m24s in the other — a 1.43x
  wall spread MEASURED between two runs of the identical calculation.
- 1.94x headroom against a 1.43x observed spread is not headroom, it is a coin flip.
```
3 h gives 2.9× the measured wall, still recovers 384 core-h, and **ceiling is not the scarce
resource right now** — the round reserves 9,515 of 21,000 after coder12's P6 change. Calendar is
scarce; a wall-killed certification costs a round. **Take the 3 h.** (Degradation is graceful either
way — `endpoint_prep.sh` has explicit per-stage budget checks and a wall kill yields a BUDGET-class
outcome the taxonomy already handles — but graceful failure still costs the round.)

🔴 **The 21-atom item must keep its 1,536/24 h.** It is the one endpoint I have no measurement for;
T21-se's cost remains RETRACTED (§R39.41); and today's convergence audit found `li_ec2_cation` at
NBasis 620 failed to converge in BOTH P5 seeds, having burned 429.55 core-h in one of them. Every
piece of evidence about the 21-atom size class says "harder than you think". Do not shave it.

## 2. 🔴🔴 I created a new mass-flip trigger while removing the old one — and it is cheaper to fix than the cap

coder12 has landed `SEI_QC_LEVEL`, `SEI_QC_MODULE` and `SEI_QC_LOGIN_PATH` into the digest
(`state.PHYSICS_ENV_KEYS`) at my request, and removed `cores_per_node` and `chain_links`. The removal
is right. **But two of the three keys I asked for are themselves environment-DETECTED**, from
`qc_env_for_jobs(env)`:
```
SEI_QC_LEVEL       from --level. NOT probed. Computation-defining. Correct to include.
SEI_QC_MODULE      from env["qc_module"], detected live on the login node.
SEI_QC_LOGIN_PATH  from env["software"]["g16"]["path"], detected live on the login node.
```
A module-version string reformat, or `g16` missing from the login PATH on one invocation, changes
these for reasons that are not computational — **every item's digest flips at once, exactly the
failure I removed `cores_per_node` to prevent.** I asked for these fields; the trigger is mine.

They genuinely do define the computation (which Gaussian binary ran), so removing them is wrong.

### 🟢 The fix is a guard, not a cap, and it is smaller than the cap coder12 offered

```
if a PHYSICS_ENV_KEY's detection returned empty/None, the digest comparison returns
"unknown" (skip, warn) — it must NEVER return "stale".
```
**An absent detection must never look like a changed computation.** The precedent exists in the same
function: `done_spec_status` already returns `unknown` when no digest is stored at all. This is the
same rule one level down, and it converts the dangerous branch (detection failed ⟹ mass re-spend)
into the safe one (detection failed ⟹ skip and say so).

**On coder12's offer to build the blast-radius cap (~20 min): spend it on this guard instead.** With
`cores_per_node` and `chain_links` out, every remaining digest field is Item-declared except these
two, so this guard covers the entire residual exposure and the cap becomes redundant. If a probed
field is ever added back to the digest, revisit the cap then.

## 3. proposer8's corrected level2 control — priced, and the SCF half is MEASURED not extrapolated

The requested probe: freq-only, both EpsInf arms, endpoint's own certified geometry via `%oldchk`,
endpoint route verbatim (`nosymm`, `Int(Grid=UltraFine)`), **only the basis swapped to level2 /
NBasis 321.**

🟢 **A lucky and useful coincidence: the P6 anchor is the SAME SPECIES at the SAME LEVEL and the SAME
BASIS** — 11-atom [Li(EC)]⁰ reduced radical, wB97XD/gen level2, NBasis 321. So the SCF half of this
estimate is a direct measurement on this exact system and basis, with no scaling at all:
```
P6 anchor, 64 threads: 171.7 s G16 elapsed, 25 SCF cycles = 3.05 core-h cold, 6.87 s/cycle
                       [MEASURED — same species, same level, same basis, same thread count]
(my derived 6.8 s/cycle from the endpoint's cycle counts matches it to 1%, which also validates
 the p = 2.2 exponent independently)
```

```
per arm                                     optimistic   base   pessimistic
Hessian / CPHF (NBasis 321, 3N=33)              8.85     11.32     14.50    [ESTIMATE, p=2.2/2.6/3.0]
SCF from a PROJECTED guess (see below)          0.60      1.20      3.05    [MEASURED upper bound]
per arm                                         9.45     12.52     17.55
shared setup + smoke + wrapper (one job)        1.66      1.66      1.66    [MEASURED]
PAIR                                           20.6      26.7      36.8   core-h
```

### 🔴 Two things about this probe that do not carry over from the main bracket

**(a) `guess=read` here is a CROSS-BASIS guess, not the same operation.** The stored density is
level3/NBasis 173; the calculation is level2/NBasis 321. G16 will project it. That converges more
slowly than the main bracket's same-basis restart — which is why the SCF line above is wider — and it
is a different operation than the one whose cost I measured. Both arms project identically from the
same `%oldchk`, so the *comparison* is unaffected; only the cost is.

**(b) 🔴 Constraint 3 CANNOT apply to this probe.** Arm F reproducing `-349.620897959` is a level3
number. At level2/NBasis 321 the energy will legitimately differ, so **this control has no
independent reproducibility anchor** — the one thing that makes the main bracket's floor a
measurement rather than an assumption. Two options, proposer8's call:
```
(i)  add a THIRD Link1 step repeating arm F identically. Its deviation from arm F is the achievable
     floor AT THIS BASIS, measured in-run.                        cost +11 core-h  ⟹ pair ~31/37/48
(ii) accept no measured floor for this probe, and report its ΔE/Δν against the main bracket's floor
     with an explicit note that the floor was measured at a different basis.   cost 0
```
I recommend (i). It is 11 core-h, it is the same "check the floor before the comparison" discipline
that caught the `%oldchk` problem for free, and (ii) requires assuming a floor transfers across a
1.9× basis change — which is the kind of assumption this round has spent its whole length catching.

🟢 **And yes to running it up front rather than conditionally.** proposer8's reason is right and it is
the one I would have given: calendar is the scarce resource, and the conditional version pays a full
round-trip precisely in the branch where moving fast matters most. ~27–37 core-h against a 21,000
guard does not justify a round of latency.

# §R39.53 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: withdrawing the `stages/` copy-back — coder12's fingerprint gate dissolved its use case

Recorded because a withdrawn recommendation that leaves no trace gets re-proposed.

§R39.50 §Q2 offered an optional `stages/` copy-back after archiving `jobs/<key>`, to restore the
cheap-resume property that my own evidence-archiving recommendation (§R39.46 §1.6) had destroyed.
coder12 has since landed the Q1 fingerprint gate, and it removes the need entirely:

```
Q1 plumbing auto-resubmit   fires ONLY when pkg_fingerprint has CHANGED
                            -> sei_stage rejects the checkpoints anyway. Copy-back buys ZERO.
(ii) spec_digest stale      fires on a plan / physics-env change -> the computation IS different
                            -> checkpoints SHOULD be rejected. Copy-back would be WRONG.
Q2 arrays                   never auto-resubmit at all.
```
**Every automatic path either implies a rebuild (checkpoints correctly rejected) or implies the
computation changed (checkpoints correctly rejected).** The tension I created was dissolved by a
different fix rather than patched by a second mechanism — worth noting as the better outcome, since
the copy-back would have been a code path that is a no-op in every scenario except one.

**The one surviving case, covered without code**: a human `--rerun`s an array item after an
INFRASTRUCTURE failure with no code change — a node dying mid-array, which is exactly what happened
to P5's t21/t22. There the checkpoints are valid and re-running from scratch costs up to **988.52
core-h [MEASURED]**. Covered by one printed line in the `--rerun` output naming the archive path and
the one-line `cp -r` that resumes from it. Zero code path, and it puts the "did anything change?"
judgement on the human who just typed a manual override.

**Also recorded**: proposer8's `deterministic` cause class (never retried regardless of build)
supersedes my `pkg_fingerprint` gate for that class specifically, and is better. My gate would have
retried an EpsInf-sentinel item once per rebuild — ~1,000 core-h of measured spend per fire, against
a class whose retry yield is zero by definition. The named cost of the stricter rule: after a real
fix lands, `deterministic` items need one manual `--rerun` instead of retrying themselves. That
converts an automatic ~1,000 core-h gamble into one typed command, which is the right trade.

**Reported to**: coder12.

# §R39.54 — engineer9, 2026-08-21: the H2 solvent smoke priced (≈0.1 core-h if it rides Round A), plus a cost risk the same probe should settle

## 1. The H2 `solvent=acetone` + `freq` probe — price depends entirely on WHERE it runs, not what it computes

`[MEASURED]` from the endpoint arm's own smoke stage: the two existing H2 smoke decks ran **5.4 s and
5.9 s** of G16 elapsed. At 64 threads that is ~0.1 core-h each. The calculation is free.

**What is not free is submitting it as its own job:**
```
                                             core-h    latency
as a standalone job                          ~1.5-2.0  one queue round-trip (57-61 s wait
  (G16 ~0.1 + job wrapper 0.85 [MEASURED]              measured, but a whole submit/collect
   + per-stage setup 0.61 [MEASURED])                  cycle in practice)
riding inside Round A's existing smoke stage  ~0.1     ZERO — answer arrives with Round A
```
⟹ **Put it in Round A's smoke stage.** This is engineer8's §R39.43 (a)-vs-(b) result recurring
exactly: the two options cost the same to *compute*, and differ entirely in round-trip structure. A
standalone probe pays the small-job tax; riding an already-submitted batch does not. Round A is about
to be submitted and already runs `sei_qc_smoke`, so the marginal cost is one extra deck.

🟢 **Free side effect worth having**: the existing smoke decks are `sp` only. proposer8's own §39.73(b)
point — *"a route smoke that does not exercise every stage the route contains is not a route smoke"* —
has been an open structural gap since the EpsInf crash, because `deck_verification.json`'s
`[VERIFIED-IN-RUN]` label says nothing about the Hessian path. **A `freq`-containing smoke deck is the
first one this package would have.** Worth building as a permanent smoke deck rather than a one-off
probe.

## 2. 🔴 A cost risk the same probe should settle at zero extra cost

proposer8's finding is that `Generic` is a row of zeros and that all the zeroed members are consumed
by nothing (`Scaled VdW` cavity does not read `RSolv`; `grep -ci cavitation` = 0; no G(cav)/G(disp)/
G(rep) anywhere) — so no B0 energy has been silently corrupted. That is a correctness result and I
have no standing to add to it.

**But it has a cost corollary nobody has priced.** Every unit cost in this document — the 2.27 core-h
Hessian, the 65.87 core-h endpoint, `u_opt`, the P5 per-species table, the entire `p ≈ 2.2` scaling
calibration — is measured under `solvent=generic`, i.e. under a PCM that computes electrostatics and
**nothing else**. If a named solvent populates that row and thereby switches on non-electrostatic
terms, it is a different calculation with a different cost, and **every anchor in this document
becomes conditional on staying with `generic`.**

**Settle it in the same smoke, for ~0.1 core-h more:**
```
run BOTH decks in the smoke stage:   H2 + eps=18.5 + freq, solvent=generic
                                     H2 + eps=18.5 + freq, solvent=acetone
record for each:                     G16 elapsed, presence of G(cav)/G(disp)/G(rep),
                                     `grep -ci cavitation`, and the full PCM block
```
If the two wall times and term lists match, every cost anchor here is solvent-label-independent and
the question closes permanently. If they do not, we have learned it on an H2 molecule for 0.1 core-h
instead of discovering it in a re-anchoring exercise later. **Total for both decks: ~0.2 core-h and
zero added latency.**

🔴 This is a cost question, not a chemistry one, and I am raising it as such: I am not asking anyone
to prefer `generic` or `acetone`. I am saying the choice moves my anchors, and the measurement that
tells us by how much costs 0.1 core-h if it goes in the round that is already being submitted.

User ruling: production moves to `scrf=(pcm,solvent=acetone,read)` + `eps=18.5`, and the entire
EpsInf bracket experiment is cancelled (design A, design C, spot-check, level2 control). Repricing.

Round A, endpoint low arm                    ~55 core-h    CANCELLED
Round A second-arm contingency               ~65           CANCELLED
Round B endpoint bracket, design (C)         ~7.3-8.6      CANCELLED

Round B level2 basis control + floor arm     ~31-48        CANCELLED
--------------------------------------------------------------------
released                                     ~110-205 core-h
```
Not a budget decision and not mine to argue. Recorded so the numbers are not later found orphaned.

**What survives unchanged**: P6 wall resize (−1,782, landed), U56-2 11-atom cert resize (−384,
gated on `u56_2.released`), the 21-atom cert at 1,536/24 h untouched, the 16-thread packing
validation (~24 core-h), and the P5 frequency recovery — whose 17/5 split and ~92–152 core-h estimate
are solvent-label questions now, see §3.

## 2. 🟢 My anchors are probably SAFE, and here is the reason rather than the hope

Every unit cost in this document was measured under `solvent=generic`. Lead is right that this is now
the main open cost question, since acetone is the production path. **But it is answerable from the
log we already have, and the answer is a pre-registered prediction, not a shrug.**

From `endpoint_tight.log`, the PCM block as G16 printed it:
```
 Atomic radii         : UFF (Universal Force Field).          <- NOT solvent-derived
 Cavity type          : Scaled VdW (van der Waals Surface) (Alpha=1.100).
 Cavity algorithm     : GePol (No added spheres)
 Solution method      : Matrix inversion.
 GePol: Cavity surface area  = 140.029 Ang**2
 GePol: Cavity volume        = 124.676 Ang**3
                        Cavity 1st derivative terms included.
                        Cavity 2nd derivative terms included.
                        RSolv  =  0.000000 Ang.
```
**Every cost-bearing quantity in PCM is already solvent-descriptor-independent:**
```
the cavity is built from UFF atomic radii x Alpha=1.100  -> does not read the solvent row
the tessera count follows from that cavity               -> unchanged
matrix-inversion size follows from the tessera count     -> unchanged
1st and 2nd cavity derivative terms are ALREADY ON       -> the Hessian already pays this in full
no G(cav)/G(disp)/G(rep) present                         -> confirms proposer8's grep
```
The solvent descriptor row supplies **scalars that enter as numbers, not as work.** `RSolv = 0` is
consumed by nothing precisely because the cavity does not use it.

🔴 **PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION**: switching `generic` → `acetone` changes the wall time of an
otherwise identical calculation by **less than the 1.43× run-to-run spread already measured on this
system** — i.e. by no amount detectable at this project's noise floor. **Every anchor in this
document then transfers unchanged: the 2.27 core-h Hessian, the 65.87 core-h endpoint, `u_opt`, the
P5 per-species table, and the `p ≈ 2.2` scaling calibration.**

**What would falsify it**, and what the H2 smoke must record for each deck:
```
G16 elapsed time; presence of G(cav)/G(disp)/G(rep); `grep -ci cavitation`;
the full PCM block including Atomic radii, Cavity type, RSolv and the derivative-terms lines
```
If `Atomic radii` or `Cavity type` differs between the two decks, the cavity changed and every anchor
needs re-measuring. If only the scalars differ, nothing does. **That is a two-line diff of two smoke
logs, at ~0.2 core-h total, riding a job that is being submitted anyway.**

## 3. 🔴 The cost item nobody has named: cancelling the bracket removed the ANSWER, not the QUESTION

The certified endpoint this project owns — the only C-8 certificate in existence — was computed at
`EpsInf = 18.5`. Under acetone, `EpsInf` comes from the tabulated row (n² ≈ 1.85), **not** 18.5. So:

```
if EpsInf is genuinely unused under equilibrium solvation (G16 prints IEInf=0, which is
  what the cancelled bracket existed to confirm)
      -> the existing certificate transfers exactly, cost 0
if EpsInf IS used
      -> the endpoint must be RE-CERTIFIED under acetone           ~66 core-h [MEASURED basis]
         and it is the C-8 gate input for every downstream item
```
**The bracket was cancelled, so this is now an unanswered load-bearing question rather than an
answered one.** The switch does not make it go away; it changes which value is in the box.

🟢 **And the H2 smoke can settle it for ~0.1 core-h more — the cancelled experiment's question,
answered at 1/500th of the cancelled experiment's price.** Run the H2 `freq` deck twice:
```
(a) solvent=generic, eps=18.5, EpsInf=18.5      (reproduces what we already ran)
(b) solvent=acetone, eps=18.5, EpsInf from the table (~1.85)
identical frequencies  ->  EpsInf is unread under IEInf=0; the certificate transfers; 0 core-h
different frequencies  ->  re-certify the endpoint under acetone; ~66 core-h, and it gates
                           everything downstream, so it must be scheduled early not late
```
🟡 **Honest limit, and it is proposer8's call whether it is sufficient**: H2 is a closed-shell
two-atom molecule with one mode and no low-frequency modes. A null on H2 is evidence about whether
the code path READS the value — the structural question — and is much weaker evidence about
magnitude on a real system. It is the same structural-null argument proposer8 used for the
single-probe design, so I think it holds, but I am not the one who gets to rule that.

## 4. What I need before I can reprice anything else

```
coder12's acetone deck change lands, then ONE smoke pair (~0.2 core-h) settles:
   (a) do my anchors transfer?          -> §2's falsification list
   (b) does the endpoint certificate transfer?  -> §3's frequency comparison
Until (a) returns, every unit cost in this document carries an implicit
"[MEASURED under solvent=generic]" qualifier, and I will state it that way.
```
No repricing is possible or useful before that, and no repricing is likely to be NEEDED after it —
§2's prediction is that the answer is "nothing changes". **Total cost of finding out: ~0.2 core-h and
zero added latency.** If the prediction fails, the re-anchoring exercise is real but bounded: the P5
per-species table and the endpoint figure are the only anchors that would need re-measuring, and both
re-measure as a by-product of work already planned.

cross-check against the P6 anchor, the per-species Hessian table, the `deterministic` retry rule, and
the U56-2 / P6 ceiling resizes.

**Scope first, so the switch is not blamed for work that was always required:**
```
endpoint_prep_reactant     certified under generic @ EpsInf 18.5   -> MUST be re-certified
endpoint_prep_product      never certified under any solvent       -> always was new work
endpoint_prep_rc_reactant  never certified under any solvent       -> always was new work

```

```
**A 10–16× branch, decided by a two-line diff of two smoke logs at ~0.2 core-h.** This is the same
freq-only-from-stored-checkpoint shape as the cancelled design (C), reused for a purpose that

that blocks a release must not be discovered late. **Put it in whatever round follows the smoke.**

The P5 frequency-only recovery runs on 17 geometries optimised under `generic`. If the production
surface is unchanged, those geometries remain stationary points and everything holds. If it moved:

the recovery's free C-9 AUDIT       does NOT survive — proposer8's point that `n_imag` diagnoses

```
So the ~92–152 core-h recovery keeps its budget justification either way, but **the argument that
raised its value at zero marginal cost is conditional on the same smoke.** Recording it because that
