# §R39.79 — engineer12 (Sonnet, replacing engineer11), 2026-08-22: PBS 23731675 wall-killed at 7244/7200s — SUBMISSION failure, not prediction failure; §R39.78 validated on items 1+2 (0.8-4.8 predicted, 1.242 core-h measured); item 3 tightened to ~2-17 core-h [ESTIMATE]; resubmit as TWO hardened hand-submitted jobs, NOT the payload path

**Handover context**: replacing engineer11 (stopped, clean handoff). Task: root-cause PBS job
23731675's wall kill against engineer11's own §R39.78 pricing, re-score those predictions against
measured reality, and produce a concrete resubmit plan for stages 3+4. Read `05_STATE.md` §1d/§2/§4
in full first, per the standing rules block. `deck_verification.json` search: **none exists for any
of the 4 ad-hoc diagnostic decks** — by design, per §R39.78 itself, these bypass the harness that
generates that file (hand-reviewed `.gjf` only, no state-machine entry). The only `deck_verification.
json` files on disk belong to real `plan.py` Items (e.g. `endpoint_prep_rc_reactant`'s, checked —
route/solvent smoke record only, no `r`/unit-cost field to misquote). No cost figure below is sourced
from a `deck_verification.json`; every number is either engineer11's §R39.78 [ESTIMATE] or a fresh
read of the raw `.log` files under `cpu_machine_pilot_results/u56_diagnostics_2026-08-21/`
(read-only, untouched — nothing was written or deleted there).

## 1. Q1 — root cause: SUBMISSION failure, not a prediction failure

`submit_diagnostics.pbs` requests `select=1:ncpus=1:mpiprocs=1`, `walltime=02:00:00`, and runs all
four decks sequentially inside ONE job with a bare `for` loop — no per-stage wall accounting, no
SIGTERM trap, no `wall_exhausted` marker, no stage chaining. §R39.78 priced item 3 ALONE at 3-30
core-h and said explicitly, in its own text: *"at 1 core: 3-30h wall, comfortably inside 48h cap
either way."* Nothing in §R39.78 ever proposed bundling all four diagnostics into a single 2-hour
job — the 48h reference throughout that section is implicitly PER JOB. Even ignoring item 3
entirely: items 1+2 alone were priced at 0.8-4.8 core-h (0.8-4.8h wall at the tool's declared
`cores_per_task=1` default) — on a good day that alone eats most of a 2h budget, leaving nothing for
an item explicitly flagged as needing up to 30h. **This is rule 6 in its purest form** (`05_STATE.md`
§4: "an author's own spec is not a spec until it has been run against a case it could fail, or read
by whoever has to implement it") compounded with the recurring "measured but not read" defect class
(same shape as three prior bugs this project already found per §1d) — the numbers were on record,
correctly derived from real per-stage log timings, and were not consulted when the PBS resource
lines were written. **Stated plainly, per instruction, not softened**: the pricing in §R39.78 was
right; the script that got submitted did not use it.

## 2. Q2 — re-scoring §R39.78 against measured reality

```
Items 1+2 (11-atom stable=opt, points idx~5/idx~20)
  predicted   0.8 - 4.8 core-h  [ESTIMATE, §R39.78]
  measured    0.514 + 0.728 = 1.242 core-h  [MEASURED, "Job cpu time" lines,
              1_point4_arc1.71/stability_probe.log + 2_point19_arc6.83/stability_probe.log,
              both "Normal termination"]
  ⟹ lands 11% of the way up the 0.8-4.8 band (barely above the optimistic floor) — well inside
  the predicted range, validating the derivation METHOD (real per-stage log timings from
  endpoint_prep_reactant, not a cube law) even though the actual outcome sat near the cheap edge
  rather than the middle. This is the same shape of result §R39.77 already produced for the
  cold-path recert — a real per-stage anchor under-predicts pessimism less than a cube law would,
  because it isn't inflating unknown physics into the exponent.

Item 3 (21-atom cation-radical stable=opt) — 8-cycle signal, partial tightening only
  observed: stage3's log (3_rc_reactant_21atom/stability_probe.log) shows route/basis setup
  (Link 101->401) completing at cpu 40.4s (line 419, "Leave Link 401... cpu: 40.4"), then SCF
  Cycle 1 through Cycle 8 running with NO "Normal termination" and NO further "Leave Link" —
  killed mid-cycle-8. Requested convergence (line 425-427): RMS density 1.00D-08, max density
  1.00D-06, energy 1.00D-06. Observed RMSDP decay across the last full cycles: 9.62D-04 (cyc 5)
  -> 3.50D-04 (cyc 6) -> 1.77D-04 (cyc 7), roughly 2-2.8x reduction per cycle (typical DIIS decay,
  not guaranteed to hold to convergence).
  Total stage-3 wall before kill: 7244s (job) - 1849s (stage1 cpu) - 2621s (stage2 cpu) = 2774s
  [MEASURED, task-brief arithmetic, independently reproduced from log timestamps: stage2 ends
  02:30:46, stage3 Link101 leaves 02:30:48, Link401 leaves 02:31:35 -> SCF cycles 1-8 window =
  2774 - 47(setup) ≈ 2727s]
  ⟹ measured SCF rate this system/level: ~2727s / ~7.5 cycles ≈ 341 s/cycle [MEASURED-anchored,
  cycle count approximate — cycle 8 itself was cut off mid-print]
  ⟹ extrapolating the observed 2-2.8x/cycle error decay to the 1e-8 RMS-density target needs
  roughly 4-10 MORE cycles [ESTIMATE — geometric decay is not guaranteed to hold at this precision;
  real SCF convergence often accelerates OR stalls near the end, this is a bounded guess, not a
  measurement] ⟹ additional 1364-3410s (0.38-0.95 core-h) ⟹ bare CONVERGED SCF-energy-only cost,
  this geometry: (2727+1364)/3600 to (2727+3410)/3600 ≈ **1.1 - 1.7 core-h [ESTIMATE, cycle-rate
  extrapolation]** — this revises engineer11's own 1.5-2.8 core-h bare-SP figure (§R39.78 §1,
  itself an [ESTIMATE] derived from opt-step timings, a different method) DOWNWARD and TIGHTER,
  a genuine cross-check from an independent method landing in the same order of magnitude.
  **Does NOT tighten the stable=opt multiplier (2-10x)** — those 8 cycles are the INITIAL SCF
  convergence, before G16 even reaches the wavefunction-stability analysis stage=opt actually
  exists to run; they carry zero information about whether the wavefunction is unstable or how
  expensive a reoptimization would be if it is. That multiplier remains genuinely unknown — it
  IS the scientific question §39.115 is asking, not a hedge.
  ⟹ REVISED item 3: 1.1-1.7 core-h [ESTIMATE] × 2-10x (unchanged, §R39.78) ≈
  **2.2 - 17 core-h [ESTIMATE], base ~7 core-h** — narrower than the original 3-30 core-h, mainly
  on the pessimistic tail (30 -> 17, a real ~45% cut grounded in a measured per-cycle rate rather
  than an opt-step-ratio proxy). Treat the 17 core-h ceiling as a tightened planning number, NOT a
  hard cap for sizing walltime (see §3(a) below — sized off a wider margin on purpose).
```

## 3. Q3 — resubmission plan, stages 3 and 4

**(a) cores and walltime, sized so a repeat kill is not plausible**

```
Stage 3 (21-atom stable=opt, endpoint_prep_rc_reactant tight-stage geometry)
  cores       4   (engineer11's own suggestion, §R39.78 §2: near-linear scaling expected for a
                   single SCF/stability calc at this size, ~zero core-h cost, cuts wall ~4x)
  sizing basis  ORIGINAL 3-30 core-h ceiling (§R39.78), NOT the §2-revised 2-17 core-h figure —
                deliberately using the wider, less-tightened bound for wall-time SAFETY MARGIN;
                the revision in §2 is a planning number, not a number to cut margin against, since
                it rests on an untested extrapolation past cycle 8

  requested walltime           16:00:00  (>2x safety factor over the worst-case-at-4-cores
                                          estimate; comfortably inside the 48h ADR-114 cap)

Stage 4 (IRC restart, irc=(restart,recorrect=never) from U56_RA_scan/irc_forward.chk)
  cores       1   (sequential path-following, no scaling claim made for this job type in
                   §R39.78 or anywhere else on this project — do not invent one)
  sizing basis  §R39.78's own 0-20 core-h range (base ~10), unchanged — nothing in today's data
                touches item 4's estimate (it never ran)

                                          comfortably inside the 48h cap)
```

**(b) one job or two: TWO separate PBS jobs, not one.** This is the direct fix for Q1's root cause,
not a new idea layered on top of it — the failure just demonstrated exactly why a shared job is
wrong: one stage overrunning starves every stage queued behind it in the same walltime budget, and
per §39.114(2) (`05_STATE.md` §1d) stage 3 and stage 4 answer independent competing hypotheses,
neither substituting for the other. Submit both, they may run in parallel if the queue allows —
they do not need to be sequenced relative to each other.

**(c) is stage 3's partial run resumable from `stability_probe.chk`? Recommendation: NO, start
clean.** What was actually checked: the chk file is 3,940,352 bytes vs 5,861,376 / 5,869,568 bytes
for the two COMPLETED `stable=opt` runs (items 1/2) — smaller, consistent with a job that never
finished writing post-SCF data (density, MOs, the stability-analysis pass), but this machine has no
G16 install and no `formchk`/`chkchk` binary available (`which formchk chkchk` returns nothing) —
**I could not open the file to confirm what SCF cycle its density actually corresponds to, or
whether it was even flushed cleanly by the walltime SIGKILL rather than left mid-write.**
`[NEEDS VERIFICATION]`, same discipline as this project's existing unsmoked-route flags. Recommend
against restarting from it regardless, on cost-benefit alone: the SCF hadn't converged (8 of an
estimated ~12-18 cycles, §2), so even a clean read only saves the ~0.77 core-h already spent — a
small fraction of the revised ~2-17 core-h full-run estimate — against a real, unquantified risk
(reading a mid-write or stale density can make G16 either error out on `guess=read` or, worse,
converge to the WRONG state silently). Trivial saving, real downside: resubmit stage 3 CLEAN, from
the already-staged `probe_point.xyz` + `stability_probe.gjf` (no `geom=check guess=read`), same as
its original build.

**(d) stage 4's route: unaffected by the kill, still valid.** Its source checkpoint is
`U56_RA_scan/irc_forward.chk` (untouched, a completely separate job tree under
`sei_pilot_work/jobs/`), copied into `4_irc_recorrect_restart/irc_forward_recorrect_probe.chk` at
DECK-BUILD time (`manifest.json: generated_at_utc 2026-08-21T11:44:37Z`) — well before this
submission ever ran. The killed job's `for` loop only ever `cd`'d into stage 3's own directory
(`3_rc_reactant_21atom/`) before dying; it never reached, read, or wrote anything under
`4_irc_recorrect_restart/`. Stage 4 can be resubmitted exactly as staged, no rebuild needed.

**(e) scratch/disk left behind — flagged, NOT deleted.** Stage 3's directory is 155 MB total: the
157,253,632-byte `Gau-53946.rwf` (the bulk of it) plus `Gau-53946.d2e`/`.int`/`.skr`/`.inp` — all
orphaned SCF scratch from a job that never wrote a valid archive entry (log itself says "Unable to
Open any file for archive entry" even on the two jobs that DID finish, so that message alone isn't
diagnostic — the missing "Normal termination" line is). Whole diagnostics tree: 176 MB. Per the
standing restriction (`05_STATE.md` §4, "never delete without the user's permission" + "never touch
`cpu_machine_pilot_results/`"), **nothing here was or should be deleted by me.** Two things for the
user: (i) once a clean stage-3 resubmit succeeds, this ~150 MB orphan set is safe to clear — that's
the user's call, not mine, and not now; (ii) this analysis only covers the RETURNED copy under
`cpu_machine_pilot_results/` — the actual compute-node `$GAUSS_SCRDIR` on the cluster itself was not
and cannot be checked from here, and a walltime SIGKILL commonly leaves scratch behind there too;
recommend the user check cluster scratch quota before resubmitting, since a second kill (even a
deliberately-margined one, per (a)) would leave another ~150+ MB orphan on the compute side.

## 4. Q4 — stay hand-submitted, hardened; do NOT move to the `U56.sh` payload path

**Definite recommendation, not a hedge: keep the resubmit hand-submitted, but harden the ad-hoc
script with a SIGTERM trap and one-stage-per-job discipline (already required by 3(b)).**

Arguments for moving to the payload were real (SIGTERM trap, `wall_exhausted` marker, stage
chaining — precisely the machinery whose absence caused today's failure) but the counter-argument
wins on a narrower, more concrete basis than "these are diagnostics by design" alone: **wiring stage
3/4 into `plan.py` as real Items is new engineering surface on top of an already-fragile mechanism
that has bitten this project twice this session** (`05_STATE.md` §1d: the `extra_env`/spec_digest
stale-resubmit trap that could auto-fire `U56_RA_scan`'s 336 core-h to repeat a known crash, and the
`payload/U56.sh` `terminal_status.json` gap that already produced a real `outcome: absent`
misreport). Today's root cause (§1 above) was never a payload limitation — it was a submission
script that didn't consult its own project's cost estimate. Fixing that requires zero contact with
`plan.py`, `spec_digest`, `cause_class`, or any of the auto-resubmit path; a SIGTERM trap in a
one-stage-per-job bash script closes the actual gap (silent kill, no marker, nothing to read until
the `.e`/`.o` file surfaces it) without adding a single new field the stale-branch machinery could
ever key on. Converting these into `plan.py` Items is real, non-trivial engineering (new Item specs,
new `criteria/`, new `deck_verification.json` generation this project doesn't currently produce for
them) for jobs whose own manifest already says, twice, "NOT a production job, not wired into any
plan Item" — that framing should stay true for this resubmit specifically because these results are
going to a human being read by hand either way (per `build_u56_ra_stability_probe.py`'s own design,
cited in §R39.78 §2), not consumed by the harness.

**Concrete hardening — what goes in the script** (two files, one per stage, replacing the single
`submit_diagnostics.pbs`):

```sh
#!/bin/sh
#PBS -V
#PBS -q normal
#PBS -N sei_u56_diag_stage3
#PBS -A gaussian
#PBS -l select=1:ncpus=4:mpiprocs=1:ompthreads=4
#PBS -l walltime=16:00:00
set -u
cd "${PBS_O_WORKDIR:-.}/3_rc_reactant_21atom" || exit 1
trap 'echo "[sei] SIGTERM at $(date), stage3 killed before completion" >> stage3_kill.marker; exit 1' TERM
module load gaussian/g16.c01.linda 2>/dev/null || echo '[sei] module load failed - continuing'
export GAUSS_NPROCSHARED=4      # keep in lockstep with the %nprocshared line the .gjf actually
                                 # carries -- coder/proposer's call whether to also edit the .gjf
                                 # itself (currently nprocshared=1, deck_meta confirms); mismatched
                                 # values are a silent-underuse risk, not a crash risk
echo "[sei] stage3 start $(date)"
g16 < stability_probe.gjf > stability_probe.log 2>&1
echo "[sei] stage3 end $(date), rc=$?"
```

(stage 4's script is the same shape: `ncpus=1`, `walltime=30:00:00`, no `ompthreads` line, `cd` into
`4_irc_recorrect_restart/`, run `irc_recorrect_probe.gjf`.) The `trap ... TERM` line is a **partial**
substitute for the payload's real SIGTERM handling — it depends on this cluster's actual PBS
signal/grace-period configuration, which I have not confirmed (`[ASSUMPTION]`: standard PBS sends
SIGTERM some seconds before SIGKILL on a walltime breach; the exact grace window is site-configured
and unknown to me — user should check with `qmgr -c 'print server'` or equivalent, or just treat the
trap as best-effort). Even best-effort, it converts "silent kill, read the `.e` file to find out"
into "a marker file names which stage died and when," which is the specific, real gap this failure
exposed — that's the whole ask, nothing more. **This does not touch `spec_digest`, `extra_env`,
`cause_class`, or `cli.py`'s stale-branch ordering at all** — the danger cited in the task brief
stays exactly as fenced off as `05_STATE.md` §1d left it.

## 4. Explicit answer to the lead's ADR-117 question

**Yes, one option carries a real repeat-failure risk, one carries a moderate one, one is low-risk —
not "none of them."** Option (a)'s reverse-direction restart is mechanically the closest analogue to
what ALREADY produced an ADR-117-class near-miss once (stage 4's silent-`recorrect`-drop risk on the
FORWARD direction, caught by critic15 before submission, never actually fired) — extending that same
mechanism to a direction it has never been run on inherits the same risk profile until it is smoked.
Option (b) is a fresh, never-run route on this cluster — "unsmoked" risk, not a "silent override"
risk specifically (no known checkpoint-state mechanism to trigger it, unlike (a)). Option (c) reuses
an already-twice-successful route and mechanism — essentially no new risk of this class. None of the
three risk any wall sized against an untested extrapolation the way T21-se's retracted cube law was —
every core-h and wall number above traces to this exact 11-atom system's own measured per-point rate,
not a scaled guess from a different atom count.

restated.

      fit the log itself flags as non-converging. A point this cheap is cheap BECAUSE no real

## 3. Candidate B cost — depends on ONE number I cannot set: the actual StepSize (or EulerPC's
effective step density), which proposer13 has not yet picked

Both options named in the spec (§39.124(2)) change how far one predictor-corrector step travels
along the arc, which directly sets how many points are needed to reach the 4.27-arc floor. I can
price the *shape* of the cost curve now; I cannot collapse it to one number without that pick.

```
Let f = (new step's arc/frame) / (0.3415, the measured default arc/frame).
N(f) ~= 12.5 / f raw points needed to clear the arc floor.  [ESTIMATE, linear scaling assumption —
  UNVERIFIED for a changed corrector; flagged, not hidden]

f = 1.0  (sanity check only — NOT a real proposal, StepSize unchanged means no fix applied)
    N ~ 13 pts   cost 13 x 1.92-3.63 = 25.0 - 47.2 core-h
f = 0.5  (StepSize halved)
    N ~ 26 pts   cost 26 x 1.92-3.63 = 49.9 - 94.4 core-h
f = 0.25 (StepSize quartered)
    N ~ 52 pts   cost 52 x 1.92-3.63 = 99.8 - 188.8 core-h
f = 0.1  (StepSize to 1/10th default)
    N ~ 130 pts  cost 130 x 1.92-3.63 = 249.6 - 471.9 core-h

Per-point cost bracket (1.92-3.63 core-h/pt) is carried forward UNCHANGED across all f — no measured
basis to shift it. The whole point of trying a smaller step is to land nearer the optimistic 1.92
end (avoid the corrector oscillation that produces the 3.63 crash rate); equally plausible per
§39.121's own standing caution ("falsifying one hypothesis does not confirm the other") that it does
nothing and reproduces 3.63/pt or a new failure mode entirely. Both ends kept live, not resolved by
argument.

Wall at 64 cores (1.8-3.4 min/pt, same G16-elapsed range as §R39.80/81):
  f=1: 23-44 min | f=0.5: 47-88 min | f=0.25: 1.6-2.9 h | f=0.1: 3.9-7.4 h
  ⟹ ADR-114's 48 h cap is not stressed until N exceeds ~700-800 points at 64 cores (pessimistic
  3.4 min/pt) — i.e. f below ~0.018, an18x-smaller-than-default step. No f in the range a "smaller
  StepSize" spec plausibly means gets near this. Wall is NOT the binding constraint for this
  candidate at any realistic parameter choice.

EulerPC: cannot be reduced to an f the same way — it is a different predictor algorithm, not a
StepSize multiplier, and G16's EulerPC characteristically takes many small internal Euler steps by
design [LITERATURE, general G16 IRC documentation — algorithm-level behavior, NOT measured on this
reaction]. If EulerPC is chosen WITH G16's default StepSize=10, the N~13/25.0-47.2 core-h row above
is the best available estimate (same target arc, unknown whether EulerPC's own per-point cost sits
inside the 1.92-3.63 bracket — no anchor). If proposer13 wants EulerPC combined with a smaller
StepSize too, use the f-table above as the point-count driver and treat per-point cost as equally
unanchored. **I cannot price EulerPC tighter than "same table, wider uncertainty" without a pilot.**

Retry: same failure/retry structure as §R39.81 — a genuine crash is cheap (bounded by points reached
before death), a "criterion satisfied on paper but arc-target undershot" silent failure (proposer12's
own named failure mode for this candidate, §39.124(2)) costs a full second attempt at the same
bracket. Budget 2x the chosen row for a worst-case single retry.

Smoke test, recommended before any full commit: 1-2 points at the new corrector setting, ~2-7
core-h [ESTIMATE from the measured per-point bracket] — both StepSize and EulerPC routes are
UNSMOKED on this cluster's G16 build (route_syntax_status class already flagged twice this project,
§1e/§R39.81); a malformed route fails at near-zero cost if caught by a 1-2 point smoke first instead
of discovered 25-470 core-h into a full walk.
```

`proposer13`'s framing (literature-sourced, not this project's own measurement): DVV is a
velocity-Verlet propagator, structurally unrelated to the Bulirsch-Stoer/DWI corrector both HPC
(Candidate B) and EulerPC ride on. That corrector was the ONE thing tying my 1.92/3.63 core-h/pt
anchor to EulerPC's cost (§R39.85 §1: "shared subsystem" argument). **That argument does not apply
here at all** — DVV shares neither a predictor family nor a corrector with anything I've measured on
this reaction. Compounding this, `proposer13` flags a SECOND unanchored axis I have not had to price
before on this work item: whether `stepsize=2` even controls DVV's step the way it controls
HPC/EulerPC's — DVV's adaptive stepping may honor it as a target, override it as a hint, or ignore it
entirely (`[NEEDS VERIFICATION]`, primary doc silent on this). **Two independent unmeasured axes
(per-point cost AND point-count-per-arc) means I cannot produce a "targeted/expected" figure the way
I did for StepSize (§R39.84) or EulerPC (§R39.85) — only a ceiling, and a wider one.** Saying this
plainly rather than presenting false precision, per the brief's explicit instruction.

## 3. The 21-atom problem — staged, cost-instrumented, NOT priced by any scaling law

**I am not producing a T21-se ceiling.** The retraction stands: the cube law was wrong in the
under-predicting direction (measured ×15.2 vs a predicted ×6.4 on a DIFFERENT, non-cation-radical
comparison), and no 21-atom cation-radical measurement exists anywhere in this project. Any number I
wrote here framed as "the 21-atom cost" would be exactly the mistake this project has already made
and retracted twice (S₂₁ cube law, then T21-se). What I CAN do instead: bound the EXPOSURE of finding
out for real, independent of any cost prediction, using a fact that requires no chemistry —
**ADR-114's 48h wall cap × 64 cores = 3,072 core-h is a hard mathematical ceiling on ANY single job
on this project, regardless of what it actually costs.** Staging turns that hard ceiling into a
series of small, sequential, informative exposures instead of one big blind one.

```
Proposed shape — SEQUENTIAL, each stage submitted only after the previous stage's real result is
read (this sequencing, not any cost prediction, IS the safety mechanism):

Stage 1: 21-atom relaxed scan (rough), submitted ALONE, first.
  Wall cap: 12h (25% of ADR-114's 48h cap — a deliberately conservative fraction, NOT a completion
    prediction; its job is to bound worst-case exposure, not estimate a finish time)
  Worst-case exposure if it hits the cap without finishing: 12h x 64 = 768 core-h (9.3% of the
    8,230.18 core-h remaining margin) — an acceptable, deliberately small cost to pay for the FIRST
    real 21-atom cation-radical data point this project has ever produced, even in a total-failure
    outcome.
  Mandatory: explicit walltime declaration (not a builder default — same standing requirement as
    every other section this round), SIGTERM trap writing a kill-marker (same pattern as
    candidate_a's own submit script), and C-13's rule applies without exception: a TRIPWIRE-ABORTED
    run still reports its real core-h, never discarded, never treated as a null result.
  DECISION GATE: if stage 1 itself hits the 12h cap without finishing, STOP. Do not submit stage 2.
    Hitting the cap on the FIRST scan stage is itself strong evidence the retracted cube law
    undersold real cost by more than a small margin — re-scope with proposer13/lead before spending
    anything further. If it finishes early, its real elapsed time sets stage 2's cap.

Stage 2: scan_refine, submitted only after stage 1 returns.
  Wall cap: sized from stage 1's OWN real result (a same-molecule internal ratio, e.g. the 11-atom
    class's own measured scan:refine ratio of ~0.865 applied to stage 1's REAL elapsed time — NOT an
    atom-count scaling, an internal same-job-type ratio, still labeled [ESTIMATE] since it has never
    been checked at 21 atoms). If stage 1 needed its full cap without finishing, this ratio approach
    is invalid — a fresh decision is needed, not an extrapolation from an incomplete run.

Stage 3: ts_opt (TS search) — the single highest-risk stage. This is the EXACT job class
  (21-atom cation-radical, open-shell) that already produced ADR-117's stage3 stability concern once
  this project. Recommend a wavefunction-stability precheck BEFORE committing to a full
  calcfc-TS-optimization+freq job, same discipline this project already has a precedent for
  (`stability_probe.log`'s pattern, ADR-115/117). Wall cap chosen the same way as stage 2 — from real
  data only, no cross-atom-count prediction.

Stage 4: IRC forward/reverse — after a validated TS exists. Given this round's finding (§1 above),
  build the reverse-arm deck with `stepsize` scaled down from the START at 21 atoms if proposer13
  judges the same corrector-oscillation risk plausible at this size — cheaper to price in from day
  one than to discover via a second crash-then-fix detour, though this is a scientific call
  (does the risk transfer across atom count?), not mine to make.

Stage 5: B+ checks — cheap regardless (11-atom B+ jobs cost 5.75-14.66 core-h each; even a generous
  multiple of that at 21 atoms is trivial against the margin).

Authorization number to hand up NOW, not a pipeline total: **768 core-h (stage 1's worst-case
  exposure) is the real number to authorize for the FIRST 21-atom submission.** Everything past
  stage 1 is priced from real data as it arrives, not pre-committed. This is deliberately NOT a
  21-atom attempt total — producing one would repeat exactly the mistake already retracted twice.
```

# §R39.90 — engineer14, 2026-08-25: guard inventory reconciliation, code-first (ADR-095 precedent
applied) — RESERVED and MEASURED are two separate, both-real ledgers in this codebase; §R39.88/89's
figures get corrected against the code, not against prose

## 0. Ground truth, read from `budget.py` directly, not inferred from prose

```python
# ResourceGuard (src/pilot_package/sei_pilot/budget.py:164-251)
self.reservations = []   # grows via reserve(), NEVER shrinks — no release()/unreserve() exists
self.measured = {}       # id -> core_hours, populated via record_measured(), SEPARATE dict

reserved_core_hours     = sum(r["core_hours"] for r in self.reservations)
remaining_core_hours    = self.max_core_hours - self.reserved_core_hours   # <- governs
                                                                              new submissions
measured_core_hours     = sum(self.measured.values())   # tracked for REPORTING only,
                                                            NEVER netted against reserved_core_hours
```

**This settles the question cleanly**: `reserved_core_hours` is a ONE-WAY, permanent ledger — once
an item is reserved, its full reservation stays locked against the 21,000 guard FOREVER, even after
it returns with a real cost far below its reservation. `measured_core_hours` is tracked in a
completely separate dict for accounting/reporting, with NO code path that ever reduces
`reserved_core_hours` in response to it. **There is no "release on return" mechanism anywhere in this
file.** This is a deliberate design (the class docstring: "예산 초과는 예외가 아니라 정상적인
결과" — over-budget is a normal outcome, not an exception), not a bug — but it means the two figures
answer genuinely different questions and must be reported as two separate numbers, never blended into
one without saying so (exactly ADR-095's lesson: label the basis, every time).

§R39.88 computed "guard today = 12,709.39 + this round's ad-hoc diagnostic charges (60.43) =

"not meaningful" caveat at the same blend I reproduced) with real ad-hoc MEASURED spend (60.43) that
never touched the reservation ledger. **Correcting**: the two should be reported separately.

```

rule 4, not because it changes a decision.
